title: Acute agitation and rapid tranquillisation (adult)
subject: psychiatry
setting: Emergency department, psychiatric ward, general ward
summary: Look for medical causes and de-escalate first; offer oral medication; if rapid tranquillisation is needed use IM lorazepam alone or IM haloperidol with IM promethazine (NICE NG10), with olanzapine or midazolam as alternatives. Use lower doses in the elderly, avoid haloperidol without an ECG or with cardiac disease, and monitor vital signs afterwards.

sections.title: Assess
items: Always consider medical causes: hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, head injury, delirium, sepsis, alcohol or drug intoxication or withdrawal, thyrotoxicosis, anticholinergic or stimulant toxicity.
Recognise early signs: restlessness, pacing, raised voice, clenched fists, threats. Grade severity and reassess after each intervention.
The aim is a calm patient who can still talk and take part in assessment, not deep sedation.

sections.title: Safety and de-escalation
items: Ensure enough trained staff, clear exits and removal of potential weapons; one staff member leads communication.
De-escalate verbally: calm, respectful and empathic tone, respect personal space, listen, offer choices, food, drink or a quiet area; avoid provocation. Continue attempts throughout.
Offer oral medication when de-escalation alone is not enough and the patient will accept it; oral is preferred over IM (Project BETA).
Use restrictive interventions (restraint, rapid tranquillisation) only when de-escalation and oral medication have failed and there is a risk of harm (NICE NG10).
Resuscitation equipment (defibrillator, bag-valve-mask, oxygen, suction) and staff trained in life support must be immediately available.

sections.title: Oral options
items: Psychotic or undifferentiated agitation: olanzapine 5 to 10 mg orally (orodispersible), risperidone 1 to 2 mg orally, or haloperidol 2.5 to 5 mg orally.
Alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, or stimulant intoxication: a benzodiazepine, for example lorazepam 1 to 2 mg orally.
Delirium: treat the cause; if medication is essential use a low-dose antipsychotic, and avoid benzodiazepines except in alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.

sections.title: Rapid tranquillisation (IM)
items: NICE NG10: use either IM lorazepam alone or IM haloperidol combined with IM promethazine. Use IM lorazepam if there is too little information to guide choice or the patient has not taken antipsychotics before.
IM lorazepam 1 to 2 mg; if the response is partial, consider a further dose after 30 to 60 minutes.

IM haloperidol 5 mg plus IM promethazine 25 to 50 mg; consider a further dose if the response is partial. Avoid if there is cardiovascular disease, a prolonged QTc, or no ECG has been done (use lorazepam instead).
No response to one option: try the other. If both have been used, arrange an urgent senior team review.
Alternatives in emergency settings: IM olanzapine 10 mg (maximum 20 mg/day; no parenteral benzodiazepine within 1 hour), or IM midazolam 5 mg (10 mg if severe) with airway monitoring.
Prescribe each rapid tranquillisation dose singly and do not repeat until the effect of the previous dose has been reviewed (NICE).

sections.title: Monitoring after rapid tranquillisation
items: Check pulse, BP, respiratory rate, temperature, hydration and level of consciousness at least hourly until there are no concerns (NICE NG10).
Monitor every 15 minutes if the BNF maximum was exceeded, or the patient is asleep or sedated, has taken alcohol or drugs, has a physical illness, or was harmed during restraint.
Use pulse oximetry when sedated; watch for respiratory depression (especially benzodiazepines with alcohol), hypotension, acute dystonia, arrhythmia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Acute dystonia after haloperidol: an IM anticholinergic such as benztropine, or diphenhydramine.

sections.title: Special populations
items: Elderly or frail: exclude delirium first; use low doses (for example haloperidol 0.5 to 1 mg or lorazepam 0.5 to 1 mg) and avoid antipsychotics in Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia.
QTc prolongation, low potassium or magnesium, cardiac disease or other QT-prolonging drugs: avoid haloperidol (especially IV); prefer a benzodiazepine.
Alcohol intoxication: benzodiazepines add to respiratory depression; do not combine IM olanzapine with a benzodiazepine (hypoxia reported).
Take account of pregnancy, physical illness, previous response, advance statements and total daily doses when choosing medication (NICE).

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Sedating before excluding hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, head injury or delirium.
Restraint that compresses the chest, neck or abdomen (risk of positional asphyxia).
Repeating doses before the previous dose has taken effect, leading to oversedation.
IM haloperidol without an ECG in a patient with cardiac disease.

drugs.name: Lorazepam
drugs.dose: 1 to 2 mg orally or IM; repeat after 30 to 60 minutes if partial response
drugs.notes: First choice if antipsychotic-naive, no ECG, or cardiac disease.

drugs.name: Haloperidol
drugs.dose: 2.5 to 5 mg orally or 5 mg IM (elderly 0.5 to 1 mg)
drugs.notes: With promethazine IM for rapid tranquillisation; ECG first; risk of dystonia and QTc prolongation.

drugs.name: Promethazine
drugs.dose: 25 to 50 mg IM, given with haloperidol

drugs.name: Olanzapine
drugs.dose: 5 to 10 mg orally or 10 mg IM; maximum 20 mg/day
drugs.notes: No parenteral benzodiazepine within 1 hour of IM olanzapine.

drugs.name: Midazolam
drugs.notes: Emergency department use with airway monitoring.
